title: Food: a recipe for disaster
subtitle: free-range, additives, half-baked
summary: Read a food label with confidence - additives, free-range, fair trade - and use the metaphors English cooks up from food, from grilling a suspect to letting someone stew.

lesson.heading: What the label tells you
lesson.text: Food production is increasingly industrialised and globalised, so knowing what our food contains matters more than ever. Adjectives like **wholesome** (good for you), 'farm fresh' and 'homemade' can be vague and meaningless, and the international numbering system for **additives** - substances added to improve taste or appearance, or to preserve food - is often incomprehensible.

examples.text: The label gave no **nutrition** information, so I didn't know if it was good for me.
examples.note: nutrition labels indicate how the food influences your health

examples.text: **Traffic-light labelling** shows high (red), medium (amber) or low (green) levels of fat, sugar and salt.
I try to make my diet as **wholesome** as possible.

lesson.heading: Descriptions with a clear official meaning
rows: foods that have had no natural features taken away and no artificial substances added
produced by farm animals allowed to move around outside, not kept in cages or stalls
not containing the protein found in wheat and some other grains
chemicals used to stop food from decaying
not treated with chemicals that preserve food or give it extra taste or colour
a way of buying and selling that makes certain the original producer receives a fair price
producing eggs or meat cheaply by keeping a lot of birds in rows of small cages
foods that are almost ready to eat or quick to prepare

lesson.heading: Who needs the information
lesson.text: Clear, scientifically accurate descriptions are vital for people with **food allergies** - the adjective is **allergic (to)** - and for vegetarians and **vegans**, who eat no animal products at all, not even eggs or cheese. They also matter to shoppers concerned about **animal welfare**, and, given public concern over bad diet and **obesity**, to everyone.

examples.text: I can't eat curry - it makes me come out in red spots. I'm **allergic** to one of the spices.
I'm a vegetarian, but I don't think I could ever become a **vegan**.
It worries me that farm animals are sometimes treated so badly - **animal welfare** should come first.

lesson.heading: Food metaphors: planning and inventing
lesson.text: A **recipe for disaster** (or for success) is a situation sure to lead to that result. To **cook up** a story or a scheme is to invent it. Something with **all the ingredients of** a hit has all the necessary characteristics. A **half-baked** plan is unrealistic or not thought through properly.

examples.text: Inviting Sophie and her ex-husband to the same party was **a recipe for disaster**.
He **cooked up** a story about his kitchen being flooded.
The film has **all the ingredients of** a box office hit.
I'm sure this is another of his **half-baked** schemes that will never come to anything.

lesson.heading: Food metaphors: people and feelings
lesson.text: To **let someone stew** (or **stew in their own juice**) is to let them worry or suffer over something that is their own fault. To **grill** someone is to ask them a lot of searching questions. Something that is **not my cup of tea** is not the type of thing I like.

examples.text: I'm not going to call him. I'm going to **let him stew** for another few days.
The police **grilled** the suspect for hours, but eventually let him go.
It's kind of you to invite me, but ballet isn't really **my cup of tea**.

lesson.heading: More food metaphors
lesson.text: To **spice up** something is to make it more lively. **Unsavoury** characters are unpleasant and morally offensive. When a relationship or a business **turns sour**, things go wrong. And **juicy** gossip is exciting and interesting.

examples.text: Let's hire a karaoke machine - that'll **spice up** the office party.
Rick has started hanging around with some **unsavoury** characters.
They started their business with high hopes but things soon **turned sour**.
Let's go for a coffee and you can tell me all the **juicy** gossip.

lesson.text: Half-baked criticises the thinking behind an idea; unsavoury criticises the character of a person. Neither has anything to do with actual food.

exercises.prompt: Six shoppers describe what they buy. Match each one with what matters to them.

pairs.left: It worries me that farm animals are sometimes treated so badly.
I want my food to be 100% natural.
I buy coffee that gives growers in developing countries a decent price.
I can't eat curry - it makes me come out in red spots.
I can't be bothered cooking - I buy ready-made meals and tins.
I never buy eggs that come from battery farms.

exercises.prompt: The label gave no ___ information, so I didn't know if it was good for me.
exercises.explanation: A nutrition label indicates how the food influences your health.

exercises.prompt: The ___ system of labelling is easy to understand with just three familiar colours.
exercises.explanation: Traffic-light labelling shows high (red), medium (amber) or low (green) levels of fat, sugar and salt.

exercises.prompt: It's sometimes difficult to find ___ foods - everything seems to contain chemicals or preservatives.
exercises.explanation: Unprocessed foods have not been treated with chemicals to preserve them or add taste or colour.

exercises.prompt: My sister has to have a ___ diet as wheat makes her ill.
exercises.explanation: Gluten-free food does not contain the protein found in wheat and some other grains.

exercises.prompt: I'm a vegetarian but I don't think I could ever become a ___. I would find the diet too restrictive.
exercises.explanation: A vegan does not eat or use any animal products, such as meat, fish, eggs or cheese.

exercises.prompt: My diet is mostly natural foods because I buy a lot of ___.
exercises.explanation: Wholefoods have not had any natural features taken away or artificial substances added.

exercises.prompt: My mother ___ me for an hour about where I had been last night.
exercises.explanation: To grill someone is to ask them a lot of searching questions.

exercises.prompt: I feel I need something more exciting to ___ my life.
exercises.explanation: To spice something up is to make it more lively.

exercises.prompt: You must fill me in on all the ___ gossip.
exercises.explanation: Juicy gossip is exciting and interesting.

exercises.prompt: Don't tell her her phone has been found. Let her ___ - perhaps she'll be more careful in future.
exercises.explanation: To let someone stew (in their own juice) is to let them worry or suffer over their own mistake.

exercises.prompt: He wanted me to go to the match with him, but rugby just isn't ___.
exercises.explanation: Something not your cup of tea is not the type of thing you like.

exercises.statement: Patience combined with interest in your pupils is a recipe for success for a teacher.
exercises.explanation: Correct - a recipe for something is a situation sure to lead to that result, good or bad.

exercises.statement: Jake's ideas are always well thought through - they are completely half-baked.
exercises.explanation: Half-baked means the opposite: unrealistic or not thought through properly.

exercises.prompt: Is each item a real food label term, or a food metaphor?

items.text: all the ingredients of a hit

exercises.answer: He has cooked up a crazy scheme for making money on the internet
exercises.explanation: To cook something up is to invent or make it up.
